title: Small interface choices can change how successfully people complete public date questions
source_unit: Census Research Report Series methodology experiment with 1,000 participants completing near-date tasks in text-entry, dropdown, and calendar designs
geography: United States; survey usability experiment with study participants

observations.period: 2026 usability experiment on near-date entry; paper published August 2026

denominator.unit: experiment participants assigned date-entry designs and tasks

effectiveness.value: calendar design performed better than text entry for effectiveness

efficiency.value: calendar design performed better than both text entry and dropdown designs for most tasks

task_condition.value: the advantage was especially relevant for near-date tasks requiring knowledge of the day of the week

perceived_difficulty.value: no design difference was observed in perceived difficulty; most participants rated all conditions extremely easy

observations.method: Randomized usability experiment comparing text-entry, dropdown, and calendar date fields across near-date tasks, including tasks requiring participants to know the day of the week.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census methodology working paper and not a population estimate or Census policy mandate. The experiment concerns near dates and its participants and tasks; it does not establish effects for distant dates, all devices, disabilities, languages, literacy levels, or high-stakes administrative forms.
observations.subgroup: 1,000 experiment participants assigned across three date-entry designs and task types; the public abstract does not provide all subgroup estimates or accessibility analyses.
observations.counterinterpretation: A design that improves measured completion can still create privacy, accessibility, device, or cognitive burdens not captured by the experiment. The lack of perceived-difficulty differences shows that people can experience all designs as easy while objective accuracy and speed differ.

related_sources.claim: A separate Census Household Panel study examines text-message contact and consent; it is related access infrastructure, not the same date-entry experiment.

boundary: This record adds an interface-design-to-public-task-completion pathway. It does not establish equal accessibility, population-level representation, trust, policy responsiveness, or downstream household and political outcomes.
